When economists explain the financial crisis that hit “tiger economies” of Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea in the late 20th century, some reach for the term “crony capitalism.” A cosy relationship between governments and firms distorted markets, leading to currency crises fueled by close ties between businesses, banks and politicians. Companies took excessive risks, safe in the knowledge that economic institutions were designed for their benefit. It was because of this rot that everything came tumbling down.

People still worry about such practices elsewhere. The idea that personal connections can yield huge advantages has led to warnings about a new age of cronyism. Some believe that protectionist policies and trade wars, whenever they arise, provide fresh opportunities for lobbying and rent-seeking. “You’re going to find the halls of power filled with special-interest groups,” one observer has warned. Markets also reflect the assumption that connections to influential figures are extremely valuable. Shares of firms linked to powerful supporters sometimes shoot up dramatically.

Trade policies often involve granting specific advantages to select firms. Early research on “the political economy of the rent-seeking society” examined how governments might issue import licences to favoured companies. These decisions did not just distort the market, they also forced firms to waste resources by competing for such privileges. A vicious circle ensued: the public noticed that profits were earned unjustly and demanded more intervention, which created more opportunities for rent-seeking. Other economists argued that rent-seeking also reduces innovation, as would-be entrants are turned off by the hassles of obtaining permits.

For all the theory, evidence of aggregate harm can be difficult to spot. Some of the fastest-growing economies in history were rife with crony capitalism. Research finds that the share prices of companies in politically connected networks can be boosted by the potential for corruption. At the same time, leaders who preside over such systems often become synonymous with impressive rates of economic growth. It remains unclear whether corruption causes poverty or simply signals a deeper institutional malaise. Some scholars even wonder if corruption ‘greases the wheels,’ arguing that deals might never occur without sweeteners.

Rich countries developed with flawed institutions, too. Cronyism and rapid industrialisation existed side-by-side in past gilded ages. In some places, “corruption evolved away from thuggery and theft,” morphing into payments made to cultivate ties with politicians. These are then formalised and legalised, perhaps through campaign finance. Instead of accepting bribes to speed up or slow down growth, elites are incentivised to allow expansion for insiders.

Recent research finds only limited evidence that cronyism benefits an economy. But though it does not grease the wheels, it rarely proves an outright catastrophe. It is hard to separate policies that favour specific firms for the greater good from those that benefit them due to personal connections. Both can distort markets and encourage lobbying.

Cronyism in any era may be bad, but it is sometimes no worse than ill-conceived industrial policy. However, mixing generous subsidies or punitive trade barriers with preferential treatment for insiders can erode public trust and competition. The cost to democracy, of course, can be far greater still.
passages.V2:
You began when egg and sperm met, and DNA from your biological parents teamed up. Your first cell copied its newly melded genome and divided to build a body. Almost immediately, genetic mistakes started to accrue.

“That process of accumulating errors across your genome goes on throughout life,” says Phil H. Jones, a cancer biologist. Scientists have long known that DNA-copying systems make occasional blunders but only recently has technology been sensitive enough to catalog every genetic error. It turns out we’re riddled with them. Every human is a vast mosaic of cells, mostly identical but cellular genomes might vary by a single genetic letter in one spot, by a lost chromosome chunk in another. By middle age, each body cell probably has about a thousand genetic typos.

These mutations—whether in blood, skin, or brain—pile up despite the cell’s accurate DNA-copying machinery and repair mechanisms. With around 30 trillion cells and 4 million dividing every second, even rare mistakes build up. Errors are far fewer in cells that give rise to eggs and sperm; the body seems to protect reproductive tissues more, ensuring pristine DNA for future generations. “The minor miracle is, we all keep going so well,” Jones says. Scientists are only beginning to explore these mutations' causes and consequences. … Many changes are probably harmless, but some influence cancers and neurological diseases. Some researchers suspect that a lifetime’s worth of random genomic mistakes underlies much of aging. “We’ve known about this for less than a decade, and it’s like discovering a new continent,” Jones says.

Since DNA’s structure was discovered in the 1950s, scientists have suspected that genetic misspellings in non-reproductive, or somatic, tissues contribute to disease and aging. By the 1970s, they knew growth-promoting mutations in some cells sparked cancers. “The assumption was that the frequency of this event was very, very low,” says Jan Vijg, a geneticist at the Albert Einstein College. But detecting these mutations was difficult. Standard DNA sequencing required large quantities of genetic material, revealing only the most common sequences while rare mutations remained invisible.

That changed around 2008, says stem cell biologist Siddhartha Jaiswal of Stanford. New techniques can now detect mutations in a tiny fraction of cells—even a single one. Jaiswal studied how mutations accumulate in blood cells before cancers develop. From more than 17,000 blood samples, he and his team found cancer-linked mutations were rare in people under 40 but increased with age, making up 10 percent or more of blood cells after 70. The mutated cells were often clones. Jaiswal figures that a blood cell-making stem cell picks up mutations that give it an advantage in growing and dividing. Over decades, it outcompetes normal stem cells, producing a large, genetically matched group. These efficiently dividing mutated blood cell clones were linked to higher risks of blood cancer, heart disease, and stroke—yet surprisingly, they were also tied to a one-third lower risk of Alzheimer’s. Jaiswal, who coauthored an article on blood cell clones' health impacts, speculates that some clones may better populate brain tissue or clear toxic proteins.
passages.V3:
Éliane Brault’s In the Shadow of the Swastika is a striking account of 1940, when Germany defeated France and French defeatists created the Vichy regime. Brault escaped prison to join the Free French Forces in London. From there, she coordinated the health and welfare of wartime refugees. … I was moved by this engaging work and began working on a full translation into English to share this well-informed narrative of France’s tragic defeat and occupation. The entire process produced considerably more than an “echo” of the original; it also revealed to me the interplay of language and history. …

The relationship between language and history is critical to a competent rendering of text from one language to another. Translators do not just translate words; they also translate a universe of discourse, a poetics, and an ideology, much of which is germane to understanding the past. Historians specialize in analyzing discursive practices over time. “Poetics” may seem an odd term in history, but it entails much besides poetry; it studies language use in all genres of writing. Colleagues will have less difficulty understanding ideologies beyond the much better known ones in politics. Translation thus subsumes critical elements of the historical discipline’s distinct manner of knowing.

Historians tend to regard translation as merely a technical skill. Articles in historical publications that address translation practices are rare. Most other remarks are cursory and concern editorial corrections, not substantive issues of fidelity to the original text or its interpretation. Yet translating primary sources requires more than language comprehension. To render Brault’s book for a non-Francophone audience, I have used my knowledge of the historiography of France’s defeat and occupation. … Otherwise, the history gets lost in translation no matter how clear the words. In short, the translation process resorts to historical practices in linguistic decisions related to people, places, and events in the text. … To verify the accuracy of both substance and style, I lean on other primary sources, the stock and trade of every historian. All the same, historians rarely learn or teach this important craft. It is relegated to specialists in foreign languages, and translators of our sources go unidentified, much less their practices discussed. Still further afield are translation studies in both theory and practice, not necessarily in any one language. Yet assessing a translation’s quality, if it occurs at all, demands a fully informed evaluation. Otherwise, malpractice can be egregious.

When evaluating such work as scholarship, the solution seems obvious. Why not include a reviewer with experience in translation from the relevant language? Many historians have rendered excerpts of their sources. Compared with modernists working in Western languages in the United States, ancient, medieval, and non-Western historians attend to these matters with more alacrity. Still better are colleagues who have published in the appropriate language. … For the sake of the general reader, however, let us also consider the implications of closely related fields of inquiry. I’m thinking here of the humanities like literary theory and of the social sciences like historical linguistics, among others. They will help us all understand better both history in translation and translation in history.

Speculative Realism, emerging in the late 2000s through thinkers like Quentin Meillassoux, Ray Brassier, Graham Harman, and Iain Hamilton Grant, challenges a longstanding assumption in modern thought: that we only have access to the world as it appears through human cognition and cultural frameworks. Instead, these philosophers argue that reality exists in its own right, independent of how we perceive or conceptualize it. The movement’s starting point is a critique of “correlationism,” a term coined by Meillassoux. Correlationism is the idea that we can never fully separate the world (or objects in it) from the ways we think about it. For centuries, Western philosophy has tended to focus on human perception, language, and culture as the lenses through which reality is inevitably filtered. Speculative Realists, however, maintain that objects, forces, and processes have their own natures, distinct from our subjective interpretations.

Why does this matter in the 21st century? One need only look to the global climate crisis for an example. Greenhouse gases trap heat, cause rising temperatures, and alter weather patterns regardless of whether we believe in climate change or not. In other words, the Earth’s systems operate independently of our debates or biases, even if those biases slow down meaningful policy action. By emphasizing a reality not beholden to human perspectives, Speculative Realism underlines the urgency of grappling with the material world on its own terms. A similar argument can be made in discussions about artificial intelligence. Algorithms learn from data and shape the digital environment in ways that can be opaque to human users. While we may interpret their functions through our own frameworks—economic, social, ethical—these systems increasingly evolve in directions not entirely predicted or controlled by humans. Speculative Realism encourages us to acknowledge the autonomy and complexity of such nonhuman forces, calling for more nuanced forms of analysis.

Critics of Speculative Realism caution against an overemphasis on the independence of objects, fearing it might sideline social and political questions. If we focus too heavily on a world that exists beyond human interpretation, do we risk ignoring important debates about power, justice, and identity—debates rooted in human interactions? Proponents respond that recognizing the reality of climate change, technology, or other nonhuman processes does not negate our responsibility to address social inequities. Rather, it offers a more balanced framework: the world’s material and nonhuman elements must be understood alongside the human-centered issues that dominate public discourse.

Ultimately, Speculative Realism points to a future in which philosophical inquiry extends beyond human horizons. It reminds us that the world’s objects—whether coral reefs or computer servers—are not merely backdrops to human drama but active participants in a shared reality. As the 21st century grows ever more complex, embracing a perspective that acknowledges both the agency of the nonhuman and our own capacity for change may prove vital. If nothing else, Speculative Realism stirs a much-needed debate about the assumptions we bring to the table when we claim to understand what “is.”

17.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Words and sentences have multiple uses depending on context. I believe and I eat have profoundly different roles as do I believe and I believed or I believe and he believes. The present tense first person use of inclinational verbs such as “I believe” normally describe my ability to predict my probable acts based on knowledge but can also seem to be descriptive of my mental state and so not based on knowledge or information. In the former sense, it does not describe a truth but makes itself true in the act of saying it --i.e., “I believe it’s raining” makes itself true. That is, disposition verbs used in first person present tense can be causally self-reflexive--they instantiate themselves but then they are not testable.
opts: Language is highly contextual, and verbs, like "I believe," can function either as expressions of mental states or as statements that validate themselves through their utterance.
The meaning of words and sentences shifts with context, and in the case of disposition verbs like "I believe," their first-person present use can be self-instantiating and not testable.

The role of inclinational verbs like "I believe" varies depending on context, as they can either describe a mental state or predict an action, sometimes making themselves true in the act of being said.
First-person present tense uses of disposition verbs like "I believe" can be self-reflexive, meaning they bring themselves into existence but are not verifiable in the traditional sense.

19.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Pregnancy profoundly reshapes the brain’s neurochemistry, with surges and declines in hormones like oxytocin and dopamine influencing emotions, cognition, and communication. When pregnancy ends unexpectedly, the abrupt withdrawal of these hormones can leave the brain struggling to recalibrate, creating conditions ripe for hypergraphia. Regions tied to deep emotion and compulsive behavior become overstimulated, making writing an almost instinctive attempt to restore balance. The words may pour out in a chaotic stream—repetitive, obsessive, spiraling—but still, they come, a desperate attempt to bring structure to grief. Similarly, postpartum hormonal shifts can trigger manic episodes in those predisposed to bipolar disorder, with hypergraphia manifesting as a symptom of this altered neurobiology.
opts: The abrupt hormonal shifts following pregnancy can overstimulate emotional and compulsive brain regions, leading to hypergraphia as a way to cope with grief and imbalance.
Pregnancy-induced neurochemical changes can result in hypergraphia, as the brain seeks stability through compulsive writing and emotional expression.
The hormonal upheaval of pregnancy and its sudden end can trigger hypergraphia, with compulsive writing emerging as a neurological response to grief and instability.
Post-pregnancy hormonal shifts can lead to hypergraphia, as the brain’s overstimulated emotional centers drive compulsive writing, sometimes linked to bipolar disorder.

There is little doubt that the mental health of teenagers, especially girls, has deteriorated sharply since the introduction of smartphones and the emergence of social media. 4. It is challenging to design studies that test if reducing social-media use can improve mental health, as trials with individual teenagers leaving while their friends remain active may yield less benefit and even cause isolation. 5. Groups of teenagers should go off social media together so that online interactions are replaced with real-world engagement.
